newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico spreads seen likely narrowing.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico spreads seen likely narrowing.

text.p: The spread on newly-issued Mexican debt should continue to narrow and the nation could reach an investment-grade rating toward the end of 1997, said Carlos Mendoza Valencia, financial director for the state development bank Nacional Financiera (Nafin).

"I would think that Mexico should come close to an investment-grade rating at the end of next year. That would imply that spreads will continue on their downward trend to levels near to what we saw before the crisis," Mendoza said in the interview with Reuters.
That could allow Nafin -- by far the largest state development bank in Mexico -- to place its issues under improving conditions.

"I think that the perception of a better risk for Mexico on the one hand and that fact that there are smaller offers (from Mexico in general) will tend to reduce the spread, and will allow us to appear with better conditions," he said.
Standard & Poor's recently raised its outlook on Mexico to stable from negative, but sovereign debt and government-backed debt such as that from the development banks is not investment grade.
Nafin has had an active borrowing plan, but its issues have tended to be smaller in size, Mendoza said.
"Our placements are not that large, as we always want them to have a good price and a volume that offers liquidity but without saturating the market," he said.
The development bank has a large number of issues coming due later this year and into the first part of next year.

"Perhaps ... that depends on how the conditions improve. We will be thinking of placements in the markets where we are already have a presence We are interested in maintaining positions with investors who are used to holding our paper."
"We will continue in the Samurai (Japan) market, in the Dragon (Far East) market, in the Euro market and in the Yankee market." "This diversification allows us to place our paper at better cost."
This year Nafin was the first emerging-market borrower to sell Eurobonds in South African rands, floating a three-year issue with a 17 percent coupon.
Mendoza noted that the development bank's large portfolio of shares, bonds and other instruments allows it to more than cover its maturing credits.
He said that despite the large number of placements by the United Mexican States this year, there is still an appetite for more Mexican paper.
"This year there was an important additional factor, that the federal government was a very active borrower and with much success, and with very large placements," he said.

"But for next year who knows? The Mexican government has fewer funding needs, and perhaps the market will be open to better demand for Mexican paper that will permit institutions like ours to go ahead with successful issues," he added.
He also noted that there was a deficit in placing Mexican paper from 1993 to 1995.
"There is still a gap to cover," he said.
